questions.scenario: In a live-coding interview you are asked to 'find accounts with more than three debits within ten minutes'.
questions.question: What is the best first step?
options: Ask the interviewer to write the solution
Clarify inputs, outputs and edge cases (time zone, exactly ten minutes, unsorted input), and walk through a small example
Start typing a solution immediately to save time
Say you would normally use an AI assistant
questions.explanation: Clarifying the problem and testing understanding with an example prevents solving the wrong problem and shows the structured thinking interviewers look for.

questions.scenario: An interviewer asks why @Transactional on a private method in your service did not roll back on an exception.
questions.question: What is the correct explanation?
options: Spring applies @Transactional through a proxy; private methods and calls from within the same class bypass the proxy, so no transaction is started
@Transactional only works with MongoDB
Rollback only happens for checked exceptions
PostgreSQL does not support rollbacks
questions.explanation: Proxy-based AOP intercepts external calls to public methods. Self-invocation and private methods are not intercepted. (Also note: by default, rollback happens for unchecked exceptions, not checked ones.)

questions.scenario: You are asked: 'Return the last three transactions for each account' in SQL.
questions.question: Which approach is standard?
options: SELECT * FROM transactions LIMIT 3
Use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY account_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) in a subquery or CTE and keep rows with row number ≤ 3
Load all rows into Java and sort them
GROUP BY account_id with MAX(created_at)
questions.explanation: A window function numbers rows within each account, so filtering on the number gives the top N per group in one query.

questions.scenario: During a project deep-dive, the interviewer asks what happens if two transfers debit the same account at the same moment.
questions.question: What makes a strong answer?
options: Say the database is fast enough
Say it never happens in practice
Explain the concrete mechanism you used (for example ordered SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks or @Version) and the test that proves balances stay correct under concurrency
Say concurrency is handled by Spring automatically
questions.explanation: Interviewers want the specific mechanism, its trade-offs, and evidence. Vague answers suggest the candidate does not understand their own system.

questions.scenario: You are preparing STAR stories for behavioural interviews at a bank.
questions.question: Which elements make a STAR answer effective? (Choose two.)
options: Giving a ten-minute history of the whole project
Focusing on the actions you personally took and the measurable result
Blaming teammates for problems to show high standards
Choosing a real situation, such as diagnosing a hard bug or raising a risk, and keeping the answer to about two minutes
questions.explanation: STAR answers are concise, real and centred on your actions and outcomes. Blame and rambling make a poor impression.

questions.scenario: An interviewer asks: 'Why should money not be stored as double?'
questions.question: Which answer is accurate and complete?
options: double cannot store negative numbers
double is too slow
double uses too much memory
Binary floating point cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so sums drift; use BigDecimal (with a defined scale and rounding mode) or integer minor units
questions.explanation: 0.1 has no exact binary representation, so repeated arithmetic accumulates errors. Decimal types or integer kobo/cents, with explicit rounding, keep money exact.

questions.scenario: You finish coding a live-coding solution with five minutes left.
questions.question: What should you do with the remaining time?
options: Say you are done and wait
Test it aloud with your example and edge cases (empty input, duplicates, boundaries) and state its time and space complexity
Start a new, unrelated solution
Rewrite it in a different language
questions.explanation: Testing and analysing complexity demonstrate engineering discipline and often reveal bugs you can still fix.
